prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Palantir Technologies Inc." (ticker PLTR), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PLTR", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Palantir Technologies Inc.
markets: Defense and intelligence software (Gotham, Maven Smart System)
Enterprise data integration and operations platforms (Foundry)
Software deployment and management for regulated/classified environments (Apollo)

mission.statement: We build software that empowers organizations to effectively integrate their data, decisions, and operations at scale.
mission.source: 2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 Business (overview statement; Palantir does not publish a separately labelled mission statement)
mission.plain: Palantir makes software that helps big organizations pull all their information together and use it to make better decisions and act on them.

about.plain: Palantir makes computer programs that gather information scattered across many systems and put it in one place. People in a company or army can then see what is going on and decide what to do. Its newer AI tool lets workers ask AI helpers to do real jobs with that information. It sells mostly to governments and big companies.
about.customers: Armed forces, spy agencies and other government departments (mostly in the US and allies) and large companies such as factories, hospitals, banks and energy firms; it had 954 customers at the end of 2025.
about.everyday: When an army plans a mission, an airline schedules repairs or a hospital manages its beds, Palantir software may be running behind the scenes.

money.plain: Software for the US military, intelligence and civil agencies (Q2 2026 share of sales)
Foundry and AIP data and AI software for US businesses (Q2 2026 share)
Defense and public-sector software for allies such as the UK and NATO (Q2 2026 share)
Data and AI software for businesses outside the US (Q2 2026 share)
AI platform that lets organizations run AI agents on their own data, sold inside the lines above

result.summary: Palantir has a strong and widening competitive advantage: its software is embedded in classified military and intelligence work and in core operations of large companies, it holds hard-to-get security accreditations, and switching away would mean rebuilding years of data integration. Its AIP platform has turned that installed base into the fastest-growing piece of enterprise AI, with Q2 2026 revenue up 93% and net dollar retention of 157%. The main weaknesses are dependence on government budgets and politics and competition from hyperscalers and frontier AI labs.

pricingPower.evidence: FY2025 GAAP gross margin was 82.4% (gross profit $3,686.3M on revenue $4,475.4M) and Q2 2026 gross margin 84.7%; net dollar retention reached 157% in Q2 2026, top-20 customers averaged $93.9M of revenue each in 2025, and the US Army consolidated purchases into an enterprise agreement worth up to $10B over 10 years, showing customers keep spending more rather than pushing back on price.

moats.evidence: Palantir is the best-known name in defense AI software and its accreditations (e.g. top-secret and IL6 authorizations) are intangible assets rivals take years to obtain; its brand is polarizing with the public, which limits some commercial and European adoption.

Foundry and Gotham sit on top of a customer's data model ('ontology') and workflows, so replacing them means rebuilding integrations and retraining staff; net dollar retention of 157% in Q2 2026 and multi-year programs like Maven show customers expand rather than leave.

There are modest effects from shared defense deployments across allied militaries (e.g. NATO's adoption of Maven Smart System) and a growing developer base, but each customer's value comes mostly from its own data.
Software economics with 82% GAAP gross margin and a 62% adjusted operating margin in Q2 2026 let Palantir fund forward-deployed engineers and AIP bootcamps that smaller rivals cannot afford.

Classified defense software is a niche with few accredited vendors and high certification costs, so programs of record like Maven and the Army enterprise agreement tend to concentrate on one or two suppliers.

Palantir sold commercial off-the-shelf software into a defense market built around cost-plus custom contracts (it sued the Army in 2016 to be allowed to compete), a model legacy prime contractors like Leidos and Booz Allen cannot copy without cannibalizing their services revenue.

Two decades of forward-deployed engineering inside militaries and factories produced the ontology approach and the bootcamp sales process that took US commercial revenue up 149% year on year in Q2 2026.
Security clearances held by staff, classified-network accreditations and long relationships with US and allied defense agencies are scarce assets, though not legally exclusive.

customers.evidence: Net dollar retention was 157% in Q2 2026 (up 7 points from Q1), US commercial customers rose 35% to 653, 220 deals of at least $1M closed in Q2 2026, and existing customers such as a multinational tech company expanded to a nearly $370M three-year deal.

talent.evidence: Palantir attracts mission-driven engineers and its alumni have founded many companies (Anduril, Addepar, Affirm's co-founders among early staff), it launched a Meritocracy Fellowship hiring high-school graduates directly, and heavy stock compensation ($684.0M in 2025) has become very valuable as the share price rose; its intense, polarizing culture deters some candidates.

product.evidence: Foundry, Gotham and AIP are widely regarded as leading platforms for operational AI; Palantir was named a leader in the Forrester Wave for AI/ML platforms (2022) and ranked first by IDC in AI software platform market share, and the Pentagon made Maven Smart System a program of record used by over 25,000 builders.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Azure AI, Fabric data platform and Copilot agents compete for enterprise AI and government cloud work (also a Palantir partner).

competitors.name: Databricks
competitors.note: Private data and AI platform (Data Intelligence Platform, Mosaic AI) competing for enterprise data integration and AI agents.

competitors.name: Snowflake
competitors.note: Cloud data platform and Cortex AI compete for where enterprise data and AI apps live.

competitors.name: Amazon (AWS)
competitors.note: AWS Bedrock, data services and classified government cloud compete for AI and analytics workloads (also a partner).

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud)
competitors.note: Google Cloud Vertex AI, BigQuery and Gemini agents for enterprise and public sector.

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: Private frontier AI lab selling enterprise agents and government AI (OpenAI for Government) directly to large organizations.

competitors.name: Anthropic
competitors.note: Private frontier AI lab selling Claude to enterprises and government; also integrated with Palantir AIP.

competitors.name: Anduril Industries
competitors.note: Private defense technology company whose Lattice software competes in battlefield command-and-control (also a partner).

competitors.name: Scale AI
competitors.note: Private AI data and defense AI company (Thunderforge) bidding for military AI programs.

competitors.name: C3.ai
competitors.note: Enterprise AI application platform selling to defense and industrial customers.

competitors.name: Salesforce
competitors.note: Agentforce AI agents and Data Cloud compete for enterprise AI budgets.

competitors.name: ServiceNow
competitors.note: Workflow and AI agent platform competing for enterprise operations automation.

competitors.name: Oracle
competitors.note: Databases, cloud and AI services for enterprises and government.

competitors.name: IBM
competitors.note: watsonx AI and consulting for enterprise and government data/AI projects.

competitors.name: Booz Allen Hamilton
competitors.note: Government contractor building custom data, analytics and AI systems for defense and intelligence agencies.

threats: Heavy dependence on US government spending (US government was 41.8% of Q2 2026 revenue): budget fights, procurement reform or a change of administration could slow awards
Frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) and hyperscalers (Microsoft, AWS, Google) selling AI agents directly to enterprises could commoditize the AI layer
Databricks and Snowflake owning the enterprise data layer and adding agent tools
Weak international commercial growth (26% in Q2 2026 vs 149% in the US) and European sovereignty concerns about buying from a US defense-linked vendor
Reputational and political controversy (immigration enforcement and surveillance work) that can cost customers, staff and partners
Key-person risk around co-founder CEO Alex Karp and founder-controlled voting structure
Very high valuation that leaves little room for any growth slowdown

ceo.name: Alexander C. Karp
ceo.background: Co-founder; BA Haverford College, JD Stanford Law School, PhD in social theory from Goethe University Frankfurt

c1.evidence: Palantir leads the emerging market for operational/enterprise AI and defense AI software, with revenue up 93% to $1.935B in Q2 2026 and FY2026 guidance of $8.150-8.158B (about 82% growth).

c2.evidence: Customers choose it because its ontology-based Foundry/AIP platform gets AI working on real operations within days (AIP bootcamps) and because it is accredited for classified work; this rests on 20 years of deployment know-how and accreditations that are hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Palantir is a household name among investors and a default leader in defense AI software, but most ordinary people do not use its products and opinions of it are split, so it is not a consumer default like Google or Netflix.

c4.evidence: Karp constantly frames Palantir's purpose as strengthening the West and its institutions (e.g. his 2025 book 'The Technological Republic' and shareholder letters), and the company accepted years of losses and controversy for defense work; a decade of this would materially shape Western defense and industry.

c6.evidence: “secretive, defense AI, surveillance, controversial, high-flying stock” — the impression is mixed: investors and defense customers view it very positively, while privacy and civil-liberties groups and parts of the public view it negatively.

c7.evidence: It rides the secular shift to AI and software-defined defense; enterprise AI and data platforms are a market of hundreds of billions of dollars, and US commercial remaining deal value grew 124% to $6.238B in Q2 2026.

c8.evidence: Its platform is horizontal and is already expanding from defense into healthcare, manufacturing, energy, finance and 'sovereign AI' deals for governments, with US commercial revenue guided to grow at least 134% in 2026.

m1.evidence: Karp argued for over a decade that software and AI would decide military and industrial power and that Silicon Valley should serve Western defense, a view now widely adopted after Ukraine and the AI boom.

m2.evidence: Karp co-founded Palantir in 2003 and has run it for about 20 years, guiding it through a decade of losses before GAAP profitability, with a founder-controlled share structure aimed at long-term decisions.

m4.evidence: Karp emphasizes customer outcomes through forward-deployed engineers working inside customer sites and talks about protecting employees' freedom to disagree, but his style is better described as mission-driven than servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Karp built a distinctive, engineering-led, anti-bureaucratic culture with forward-deployed engineers that produced Gotham, Foundry, Apollo and AIP in succession.

m6.evidence: Karp is deeply involved in product strategy and customer deals but is trained in law and philosophy, not engineering; product engineering leadership comes from CTO Shyam Sankar and co-founders.

m7.evidence: Karp clearly cares about a cause beyond profit (defending Western democracies) and pledged support to Ukraine early, but his work on surveillance and immigration enforcement makes judgments of his character divisive.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Alex Karp at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Karp is one of the most recognizable CEOs: frizzy hair, Tai Chi and cross-country skiing, combative philosophical earnings calls and the book 'The Technological Republic'.

m9.evidence: Under Karp revenue rose from $1,092.7M in 2020 to $4,475.4M in 2025 and operating income swung from a $1,173.7M loss to a $1,414.0M profit, with Q2 2026 revenue up 93%.

m10.evidence: Palantir is not known for frugality: stock-based compensation was $684.0M in 2025 and it has paid very high executive pay, although it runs with relatively few employees (4,429 at end of 2025).

c10.evidence: Its software helps hospitals, factories, militaries and governments (e.g. NHS Federated Data Platform, Ukraine's defense), affecting many people indirectly, but it is used by organizations rather than directly improving the daily lives of billions.

p2.evidence: Integrating messy data across thousands of systems and running AI on it securely in classified and life-critical settings is extremely hard and matters for national security and core industry.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin rose from 67.7% in 2020 to 82.4% in 2025 and operating margin from -107.4% to +31.6%.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Palantir had $9,409.1M of cash and marketable securities, no borrowings on its balance sheet and stockholders' equity of $9,774.2M.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from -$1,173.7M (2020) to $1,414.0M (2025) and operating cash flow from -$296.6M to $2,134.5M.

v1.evidence: For defense and complex operational AI it is widely seen as the best (it gets AI into real workflows in days, on classified networks), but for general data warehousing or simple AI uses Microsoft, Databricks or Snowflake are credible alternatives.

v2.evidence: Its mission and alumni network attract strong engineers and its stock has made pay very valuable, but it does not appear near the top of major employer rankings and its culture is polarizing; no verified top-tier ranking could be found.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, the US and allied militaries (Maven Smart System, Army enterprise agreement), the UK NHS and many manufacturers would lose core operating software and notice immediately, though critics argue its surveillance uses make the world less free.
